newsitem.title: USA: NYC studies whether drivers pay insurers too much.
newsitem.headline: NYC studies whether drivers pay insurers too much.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, questioning whether insurers are overcharging drivers by not passing along the benefit of a sharp fall in car thefts, set up a task force Friday to examine the issue.

The group, which will be chaired by Jose Maldonado, the Commissioner of the Department of Consumer Affairs, will compare the rates paid by New York City residents with those paid by state residents who live in other areas.

If the group, which has 60 days to complete its work, finds that comprehensive automobile insurance rates in the city do not reflect the drop in car thefts, it will propose "remedial action," the mayor said, in prepared remarks.
Giuliani, who considers lower crime rates one of his Administration's biggest accomplishments, did not disclose what types of recommendations the task force might make.
In a preliminary report, the Consumer Affairs Department found that in New York City a total of 71,543 cars were reported stolen in 1995, down sharply from 146,925 in 1990.
Yet from 1990 to 1994, the average premium for comprehensive auto insurance in New York state rose to $187.36, a 22 percent rise from $153.52.
And from 1990 to the third quarter of 1995, insurers paid fewer claims to New York state drivers, with the amount dropping 17 percent to $358.2 million from $429.4 million.
"It is time to ask why New Yorkers have not benefited from declining auto theft rates," Giuliani said.
